title: Loan Covenants: Staying Inside the Ratios Your Lender Set
summary: Loan covenants set the ratios your lender tests and the reporting you owe. Learn how to forecast your headroom and see a breach coming months ahead.
body_markdown:
## What Loan Covenants Are and What They Require of You


Loan covenants are the conditions in a credit agreement that a borrower has to keep satisfying for the entire life of the facility. They fall into three families: affirmative covenants (what you must do), negative covenants (what you can’t do without lender consent), and financial covenants (the ratios you have to hold at each test date).


Here’s what owners find out the hard way. You can pay every invoice and every principal payment on time, close a quarter you’re satisfied with, and still breach. A breach doesn’t require a missed payment. It takes one number landing on the wrong side of a line on a reporting date, because a covenant is a promise that converts into a lender control right the moment it’s broken.


One number, on one date.


**Affirmative covenants** are the operating hygiene the agreement requires. Deliver quarterly internal statements and an annual audited or reviewed set by stated deadlines. Deliver a signed compliance certificate with the ratio math shown. Keep insurance in force, stay current on federal, state, and local taxes, maintain your licenses and permits, give notice of litigation or a material adverse change or a default itself, often within five business days, and permit field exams and collateral audits.


**Negative covenants** are the actions that need written consent. Typical restrictions cover additional indebtedness, liens on pledged assets, mergers and asset sales outside the ordinary course, acquisitions above a basket limit, transactions with affiliates, a cap on annual capital expenditures, and restricted payments. Restricted payments is the clause an owner should read first. It governs distributions, dividends, and equity redemptions.


**Financial covenants** are the ratios. The five financial covenants explained below are the ones a commercial bank most often tests on a privately held company.


- **Fixed charge coverage ratio (FCCR).** Cash earnings available for fixed obligations over those obligations. One agreement filed with the SEC runs covenant EBITDA minus capital expenditures minus cash income taxes over scheduled cash principal plus cash net interest. A 1.20 to 1.00 minimum is common in middle-market deals.
- **Debt service coverage ratio (DSCR).** Cash flow available for debt service over principal plus interest only. Whether capital expenditures and cash taxes sit above or below the line can be the whole margin of compliance for a capital-intensive business.
- **Leverage ratio, or funded debt to EBITDA.** Total funded debt over covenant EBITDA, with a maximum that steps down over the life of the loan. It usually drives the pricing grid too, so it sets your interest margin as well as your compliance.
- **Minimum tangible net worth.** Equity minus intangibles, often minus amounts due from owners and affiliates, with a floor that builds each year by a percentage of net income. This is the covenant that quietly makes a large owner distribution a compliance event.
- **Minimum current ratio or minimum liquidity.** Current assets over current liabilities, or a dollar floor of unrestricted cash plus revolver availability. Asset-based facilities add a borrowing base certificate and an availability block, tying compliance to the receivables and inventory cycles behind[working capital optimization](https://www.indinero.com/blog/working-capital-optimization/) .


Bank facilities for private companies are almost always maintenance-tested, so the ratio gets measured on a schedule whether or not you do anything. Incurrence-tested covenants only measure when you act, such as borrowing more or making a distribution. Covenant practice guides, including Simpson Thacher’s Leveraged Finance 101 covenant handbook, draw that line carefully. Most owner-led businesses live under maintenance tests, so assume the clock runs on its own.


## Why a Covenant Breach Costs More Than a Missed Ratio


A covenant breach costs more than the ratio because it converts a reporting miss into a set of lender rights and accounting outcomes you never priced. The ratio is the trigger. The cost is everything the trigger sets in motion.


**Acceleration and the right to stop funding.** A breach creates an event of default, which typically lets the lender declare the entire balance immediately due. A commercial bank rarely accelerates a performing borrower over a first technical breach. What it can do immediately is more disruptive. It can block further draws on the revolver. A business that funds payroll and inventory from a line of credit can lose its working capital the same week its covenant math fails, even though collections never changed. That’s one reason[cash flow forecasting](https://www.indinero.com/blog/cash-flow-forecasting-for-growing-businesses/) and covenant monitoring belong in one model.


**Cross-default.** Most agreements define an event of default to include a default under any other material debt agreement. One breach on a term loan can trip the revolver, the equipment financing, and a capital lease at once. One number, several facilities. A single tight covenant inside the smallest facility can create the largest problem.


**Reclassification from long-term to current.** This is the consequence owners underestimate most, and it isn’t a negotiation. It’s an accounting outcome. Under ASC 470-10-45-11, current liabilities include long-term obligations that are or will be callable by the creditor because the borrower violated a provision of the debt agreement at the balance sheet date, or because a violation not cured within a grace period will make it callable ([FASB, classification of debt in a classified balance sheet](https://storage.fasb.org/Prop_ASU_(Rev)-Debt_(Topic_470)-Simplifying_the_Classification_of_Debt_in_a_Classified_Balance_Sheet_(Current_versus_Noncurrent).pdf) ). One narrow escape exists. The borrower gets a waiver meeting the conditions in ASC 470-10-45-1 and 470-10-45-11(a), including a waiver of the right to call the debt for more than one year, before the statements are issued or available to be issued. A 30-day waiver doesn’t save the classification.


Then the second-order effect lands. Move a term loan from long-term to current and current liabilities jump, which collapses your current ratio, which can breach a current ratio covenant you were comfortably passing. One breach manufactures a second out of pure presentation.


**Going-concern exposure.** ASC 205-40 requires management to evaluate every reporting period whether substantial doubt exists about the entity’s ability to continue as a going concern within one year after the statements are issued or available to be issued. Its list of adverse conditions includes loan defaults, debt restructuring undertaken to avoid default, working capital deficiencies, and negative operating cash flows. Management’s plans count against that doubt only when they’re probable of being implemented and probable of mitigating the condition. So a breach plus accelerated principal isn’t only a bank conversation. It can force a footnote that travels to every surety, landlord, insurer, and large customer that reads your statements.


**The waiver bill.** A waiver is a purchase, and the bank sets the price. Publicly filed amendments show the usual components.


- An amendment or waiver fee on outstanding principal plus unused commitments. Routine one-off waivers commonly land in the range of 25 to 50 basis points, and repeat or severe breaches price higher.
- A margin step-up on the interest rate, sometimes permanent rather than temporary.
- Tightened covenant levels going forward. The bank rarely resets you to where you were. It resets you to a level you only just clear.
- Added reporting. Monthly compliance certificates instead of quarterly, a rolling 13-week cash flow forecast, monthly borrowing base certificates, sometimes a field exam at your expense.
- Shrunken baskets. Lower caps on capital expenditures, acquisitions, and restricted payments. Owner distributions are often the first thing suspended.


The non-financial cost lasts longest. A waiver converts your lender from a counterparty into a supervisor, and the reporting burden usually outlives the breach that caused it.


## How to Monitor and Forecast Covenant Headroom


Covenant headroom is the distance between where a ratio sits today and the level that breaches it, stated as the percentage decline in the driver that would get you there. Monitoring it takes three artifacts: a compliance certificate prepared as a calculation, a standing covenant EBITDA bridge, and headroom carried inside the rolling forecast.


### The compliance certificate is a calculation, not a form


Most bank agreements require a signed compliance certificate alongside quarterly internal statements, generally within 45 days of quarter end, and alongside annual audited or reviewed statements, generally within 90 to 120 days of fiscal year end. Tighter or asset-based facilities add monthly internal statements within about 30 days plus a monthly borrowing base certificate. A financial officer signs it, and it shows the arithmetic for each financial covenant, line by line, against the required level.


Three things go wrong with it in practice. It gets treated as paperwork and built from the trial balance in the last two days before the deadline, by which point the quarter is closed and the number is whatever it is. It gets calculated on the P&L definition of EBITDA rather than the credit agreement’s definition, and that gap is often the whole difference between passing and failing. And nobody re-reads the definitions, which get amended. The trailing period, the add-back cap, and the treatment of capital expenditures can all change in an amendment nobody re-circulated internally.


### The covenant EBITDA bridge


Your credit agreement doesn’t use EBITDA. It uses a defined term, usually Consolidated EBITDA, that starts from consolidated net income under GAAP and then adds back a negotiated list. A 2024 financing agreement filed with the SEC shows the structure cleanly. Consolidated EBITDA equals consolidated net income plus, without duplication, net interest expense and letter of credit fees, depreciation and amortization, extraordinary or unusual or non-recurring charges, non-cash charges, restructuring and integration costs, and transaction fees. Then it caps the discretionary portion. Capped Adjustments can’t exceed 12.5% of Consolidated EBITDA before add-backs for the first eight quarters after the effective date, and 10% for each test period thereafter ([SEC EDGAR, 2024 financing agreement, exhibit 10.1](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/716643/000119312524167408/d769948dex101.htm) ).


Private credit agreements commonly carry 15 to 30 or more defined adjustments, which is why the bridge has to be a standing schedule rather than a quarterly reconstruction. Here it is on illustrative figures, in thousands.


Line Amount


GAAP net income 1,250


Plus interest expense 620


Plus income tax expense 430


Plus depreciation and amortization 980


**Reported EBITDA** **3,280**


Plus one-time legal settlement 140


Plus ERP implementation costs 110


Plus non-cash equity compensation 90


Less add-backs above the 10% cap (cap = 328) (12)


**Covenant EBITDA** **3,608**


The capped-adjustment line is the detail that gets missed. The company claimed 340 of add-backs against a cap of 328, so 12 is disallowed and covenant EBITDA is 3,608 rather than 3,620. Small on its own. Not small once you compute headroom.


### Carrying headroom in the rolling forecast


Stating headroom as a percentage decline is what makes it forecastable. It turns a compliance threshold into an operating tolerance leadership can manage against.


Run it on the bridge above. The FCCR numerator is covenant EBITDA of 3,608 minus maintenance capital expenditures of 700 minus cash income taxes paid of 380, which equals 2,528. The denominator is scheduled cash principal of 1,400 plus cash interest of 620, which equals 2,020. That puts the fixed charge coverage ratio at 1.25x against a required minimum of 1.20x.


Now find the breach point. The numerator has to stay at or above 1.20 times 2,020, which is 2,424. It sits at 2,528, so the cushion is 104. On covenant EBITDA of 3,608, that is a 2.9% decline before breach.


Then test the other covenant. Funded debt of 11,500 over covenant EBITDA of 3,608 gives a leverage ratio of 3.19x against a maximum of 3.50x. Covenant EBITDA could fall to 3,286 before that one breaks, an 8.9% decline.


Leverage looks like the risky covenant because it’s the one that sounds strategic. The binding covenant here is FCCR, and it binds at a 2.9% earnings decline. One soft quarter, one delayed price increase, or one input-cost increase you absorbed instead of passing through gets you there.


The covenant that binds isn’t the one leadership watches.


A forecast that carries covenants well has six features.


1. **A covenant tab inside the rolling forecast, not a separate file.** Every projected period carries the bridge, each ratio, the required level, and headroom as a percentage. It’s one of the practical reasons[a rolling forecast beats a static annual budget](https://www.indinero.com/blog/financial-forecasting-rolling-vs-static/) , and it should run four to six quarters out.
2. **Step-downs mapped on a calendar.** Required levels tighten on dates. A 3.50x maximum that becomes 3.25x two quarters out means the covenant comes to you, and nothing in your results has to change for you to fail.
3. **A downside case run against the weakest quarter, not the average.** Seasonal businesses breach in their trough, and annualized math hides it. Test the trailing period that ends on your worst quarter.
4. **Each covenant’s actual driver named.** FCCR is driven by cash capital expenditures and scheduled amortization as much as by earnings. A purchase that improves the business can fail the covenant that measures your ability to fund it.
5. **Headroom priced into the decision before it’s made.** Run the equipment purchase, the expansion, or the owner distribution through the covenant model first. A restricted-payments basket and a tangible net worth floor can turn a distribution the business can clearly afford into one the agreement won’t permit, which is why[capital allocation](https://www.indinero.com/blog/capital-allocation-strategy/) and covenant compliance can’t be separate conversations.
6. **A written trigger threshold.** Pick a level, say headroom below 10%, that automatically starts an early lender conversation. Approaching a lender a quarter ahead with a plan is a different conversation than disclosing a breach after it happened.


If the books can’t support that cadence, it’s a close problem before it’s a forecasting problem. Fix the close first. The covenant model is only as good as the trial balance under it.


## What Disciplined Covenant Management Looks Like


Disciplined debt covenant compliance looks like a monthly number, a mapped calendar of step-downs, and a lender conversation you start rather than receive. Current credit conditions argue for that discipline rather than against it.


Terms aren’t loosening for businesses this size. In the April 2026 Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey, covering the first quarter, the Federal Reserve reported that moderate to modest net shares of banks had tightened loan covenants along with higher premiums on riskier loans and tighter collateral requirements, for firms of all sizes, and that tightening banks cited a less favorable or more uncertain economic outlook, worsening industry-specific problems, and reduced tolerance for risk ([Federal Reserve, April 2026 Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey](https://www.federalreserve.gov/data/sloos/sloos-202604.htm) ). By the July 2026 survey, standards were basically unchanged on net for commercial and industrial loans to firms of all sizes. Conditions stabilized. The terms that tightened were not given back.


Regional data points the same direction. The Kansas City Fed’s small business lending survey for the first quarter of 2026 found roughly 10% of respondents tightening credit standards on net, continuing a long-term trend across the past four years, with all loan terms tightening and about 76% of tightening banks citing worsening industry-specific problems ([Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City, Small Business Lending Survey, Q1 2026](https://www.kansascityfed.org/surveys/small-business-lending-survey/small-business-lending-q1-2026/) ).


Most established businesses this size are already inside a covenant structure. The Federal Reserve’s 2026 Report on Employer Firms found 69% of employer firms carried outstanding debt, and among firms with debt, 59% had provided a personal guarantee and 51% had pledged business assets as collateral ([2026 Report on Employer Firms, Small Business Credit Survey](https://www.fedsmallbusiness.org/reports/survey/2026/2026-report-on-employer-firms) ). Sit with the personal guarantee figure for a moment. In most of these structures a breach isn’t only a company problem.


Margin pressure is the live threat to headroom. The same report found rising costs of goods, services, and wages was the most commonly reported financial challenge, and 77% of firms faced one or both cost-related challenges. Covenants get tested on earnings, and earnings are being squeezed by input costs. That’s the arithmetic behind most covenant surprises right now, and it’s why[a KPI dashboard leadership actually reads](https://www.indinero.com/blog/kpi-dashboards-for-business-leaders/) should carry headroom next to margin.


**Signals that covenant management has drifted:**


- The compliance certificate gets assembled in the final days before the deadline from whatever the trial balance says.
- Nobody on the leadership team can state current headroom on each covenant without opening a file.
- Covenant EBITDA is produced fresh each quarter instead of maintained as a standing bridge.
- The forecast projects revenue, margin, and cash, but not ratios.
- A capital purchase or owner distribution was approved before anyone checked the restricted-payments basket, the capital expenditure cap, or the tangible net worth floor.
- The agreement has been amended and the current definitions were never re-read against the model.
- The last covenant conversation with the bank was started by the bank.


**A cadence that holds up:**


- **Monthly.** Close the books, refresh the covenant bridge and each ratio on actuals, update headroom percentages.
- **Quarterly.** Prepare and reconcile the compliance certificate, re-forecast four to six quarters out including scheduled step-downs, run the downside case against the trough quarter.
- **Before any material capital decision.** Run it through the covenant model and the negative covenant baskets first.
- **Annually, and after any amendment.** Re-read the definitions, the test periods, the add-back caps, and the cure provisions against the model.

Indinero treats loan covenants as a continuous discipline rather than an event, because the ratios get tested on a schedule for as long as the facility exists. You aren’t modeling one decision. You’re carrying a forward view of the ratios so a tight quarter is visible months out instead of on a certificate deadline. Three layers have to line up for that to work.


**The books have to close on a cadence the covenants can be measured against.** Covenant math is only as reliable as the trial balance under it. Accrual cutoffs, revenue recognition, inventory, and capitalization policy all move covenant EBITDA directly, and they also move tangible net worth and the current ratio. When the close slips or the policies drift, the compliance certificate becomes a guess signed by an officer. If that’s the gap, the fix is to strengthen the accounting function first, and[indinero’s accounting services](https://www.indinero.com/services/accounting-services/) exist for exactly that. The CFO layer sits on top of it rather than beside it.


**The reporting layer has to show the ratios, not just the statements.** Covenant levels, actual ratios, headroom as a percentage, and the covenant EBITDA bridge belong on the monthly report leadership already reads, not in a separate compliance binder somebody maintains. Owners should be able to answer “how close are we” in one look, and the answer should be a number with a date on it.


**The forecast has to carry covenants as outputs.** A rolling forecast that projects revenue, margin, working capital, and cash but stops short of the ratios leaves the most consequential constraint on the business outside the model. A CFO-led forecast runs the covenant calculation in every projected period, under a base case and a credible downside, and flags the first period where headroom crosses the trigger threshold.


The CFO role here stays strategic. It uses the numbers. It doesn’t produce them. With[indinero’s CFO services](https://www.indinero.com/services/cfo-services/) , that shows up in four places.


1. **Translating the credit agreement into an operating constraint leadership can use.** A Consolidated EBITDA definition with 20-plus add-backs and a 10% cap is a legal document. Turning it into one monthly number with a headroom percentage beside it is the work.
2. **Making the binding covenant visible.** As the illustration above shows, the covenant that breaks often isn’t the one leadership assumes. Knowing FCCR binds at a 2.9% earnings decline while leverage binds at 8.9% changes which lever you reach for first.
3. **Pricing covenant impact into capital decisions before they’re committed.** The equipment purchase, the new facility, the hiring plan, the owner distribution. Each carries a covenant consequence, and the useful time to know it is before the owner or the board approves it.
4. **Changing the character of the lender conversation.** Headroom that’s forecast, documented, and brought to the bank a quarter ahead gets handled as risk management. The same number disclosed after the test date gets handled as a default, and priced like one.


Engagements are fractional and scoped to the complexity a business actually carries, so you get senior financial leadership without the cost or commitment of a full-time CFO hire. That’s backed by continuous operations since 2009 and 500+ regular customers across industries. One boundary worth stating plainly: if the business needs a different or larger facility, that’s a separate exercise from covenant management and outside what we’re covering here.


None of this makes a breach impossible. Demand shifts, a customer concentration goes wrong, an input cost moves faster than you can reprice it. The point is to replace surprise with lead time, because lead time is what buys you options. If you’d like to see what that looks like against your own agreement, reach out for a free consultation. We’d like to understand how your facility is structured and where your headroom actually sits.


## Frequently asked questions


Owners and leadership teams tend to land on the same handful of questions once they start reading their own credit agreement closely. Here are the ones that come up most.


### What is the difference between an affirmative, a negative, and a financial covenant?


Affirmative covenants are what you must do, negative covenants are what needs lender consent, and financial covenants are the ratios you have to hold. Affirmative duties cover reporting deadlines, signed compliance certificates, insurance, and staying current on taxes. Negative covenants restrict new debt, liens, acquisitions, capital expenditures, and restricted payments, which is the clause governing owner distributions. Financial covenants get measured on a schedule whether or not you act, so the clock runs on its own.


### Which financial ratios do lenders most commonly test?


Lenders most commonly test fixed charge coverage, debt service coverage, leverage or funded debt to EBITDA, tangible net worth, and a current ratio floor. A 1.20 to 1.00 fixed charge coverage minimum is common in middle-market deals, and leverage maximums usually step down over the life of the loan. The definition matters more than the list, because your agreement uses a negotiated Consolidated EBITDA rather than the P&L version. That gap often decides whether you pass.


### What actually happens to a business that trips a covenant?


Tripping a covenant creates an event of default, which lets the lender block further revolver draws, accelerate the balance, and reprice the facility. A bank rarely accelerates a performing borrower over one technical breach. Blocking draws is faster and more disruptive, because a business funding payroll from a line of credit can lose its working capital the same week. Cross-default clauses can trip other facilities at once, and ASC 470 can reclassify the debt from long-term to current.


### How far ahead can a business see a covenant problem coming?


A rolling forecast that carries each covenant calculation can show a tight quarter four to six quarters ahead of the test date. The useful form is headroom stated as the percentage decline in the driver that would cause a breach, which turns a threshold into an operating tolerance. Indinero’s CFO Services run that calculation in every projected period under a base case and a credible downside, and flag the first period that crosses your trigger threshold.


### Can a lender waive a breach, and what does a waiver usually cost?


Yes, lenders routinely waive covenant breaches, and the waiver is priced like a purchase through a fee, a higher margin, and tighter terms. The bank rarely resets covenant levels to where you were. It resets them to a level you only just clear, and it usually adds reporting like monthly compliance certificates or a 13-week cash forecast. Baskets shrink too, and owner distributions are often the first thing suspended.


### How do covenants constrain decisions like a large purchase or an owner distribution?


Covenants can block a purchase or distribution the business can clearly afford, through capital expenditure caps, restricted-payments baskets, and tangible net worth floors. A tangible net worth floor that builds each year by a share of net income makes a large owner distribution a compliance event. Fixed charge coverage is driven by cash capital expenditures as much as earnings, so a purchase that improves the business can fail it. Indinero’s CFO Services model that consequence before the owner or board approves the spend.
